terms.gloss: emotion, a stirring of the mind
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.136 (Lewis & Short): mōtūs animī nimiī
terms.comment: Cicero’s plain expression, neither good nor bad; in the plural, animī mōtūs, the emotions. Traupman: animī mōtūs exprimere, to express one’s emotions.

evidence: Quīnt. 6.2.8 (Lewis & Short): adfectuum duae sunt speciēs
Phaedr. 3 prol. 33–37: affectūs propriōs in fābellās trānstulit
terms.comment: In Cicero a state or disposition of mind; the sense “emotion, passion” is Quintilian’s and later prose’s, and in the post-Augustan writers it is often fondness, love (Lewis & Short).

Cicero’s word for the Stoics’ πάθη, the emotions that unsettle the mind: grief, fear, desire, joy out of measure. So not a neutral word for a feeling; elsewhere it is confusion, disorder (Lewis & Short).
Exprimere, “press out”, is also “portray, express” (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: feelings, especially of anger or pride

phrases.latin: servitūs obnoxia, quia quae volēbat nōn audēbat dīcere, affectūs propriōs in fābellās trānstulit
phrases.english: the slave, who did not dare say what he wanted, put his own feelings into fables

phrases.latin: circā movendōs adfectūs in hoc posita est, ut moveāmur ipsī
phrases.english: the secret of stirring the emotions lies in being moved ourselves

sources: Lewis & Short: motus · Lewis & Short: affectus · Lewis & Short: perturbatio
